title: 5 Best Health Savings Accounts of 2026 — Top HSAs Compared
description: Compare the 5 best HSAs of 2026 by fees, investment options, and interest rates. Find the right health savings account to cut your tax bill.
lede: A health savings account can shave thousands off your annual tax bill — but only if you pick one with low fees and solid investment options. The difference between a great HSA and a mediocre one compounds year after year, especially if you're using the account as a stealth retirement vehicle. We tested five leading HSAs on fees, investment lineup, interest rates, and ease of use to help you choose the right one.

sections.heading: How to choose the right HSA
paragraphs: Not all HSAs are created equal. Custodian fees, minimum balances before investing, and fund choices vary wildly — and a $3/month fee sounds trivial until you realize it devours $36 a year in interest before you've grown a cent.

subsections.heading: Fees and account minimums
paragraphs: Monthly maintenance fees range from $0 to nearly $4. Over a decade, a $3.95/month fee costs you roughly $500 before compounding — money that could have been invested. Look for accounts that waive fees when you maintain a minimum balance, and check whether that minimum is held in cash (earning little) or can sit in your investment portfolio.

subsections.heading: Investment options
paragraphs: The real HSA advantage is triple-tax savings: contributions go in pre-tax, growth is tax-free, and qualified withdrawals are tax-free. That only pays off if you can invest beyond a low-yield savings balance. Check the fund menu for low-cost index funds — look for expense ratios under 0.10% — and confirm how much cash you must hold before investing.

subsections.heading: Interest rates on uninvested cash
paragraphs: If you use your HSA as a pass-through for current medical expenses rather than a long-term investment account, the APY on your cash balance matters. Rates fluctuate with the Fed, but comparing base rates across providers reveals meaningful differences — some custodians pay almost nothing while others pass along competitive yields.

subsections.heading: FDIC or NCUA insurance
paragraphs: Your cash balance should be FDIC-insured up to $250,000. Most bank-based HSAs meet this standard, but confirm it, especially with newer fintech-style providers. Investments held in brokerage accounts are covered by SIPC, not FDIC, which protects against custodian failure — not market losses.

subsections.heading: Integration with your health plan and employer
paragraphs: If your employer contributes to your HSA, your HR department may require a specific custodian. Check before opening an outside account — you can always do a trustee-to-trustee transfer later, but the process takes weeks and may incur a transfer fee. Also verify the provider's mobile app and debit card usability if you plan to pay medical bills directly.

sections.heading: Bottom line
paragraphs: Fidelity and Lively stand out for fee-conscious savers who want real investment access without sacrificing cash yield. If your employer uses Optum or HealthEquity, the locked-in custodian is fine for contribution purposes — just consider a trustee-to-trustee transfer to a free provider once your balance grows. Further HSA is a reasonable middle ground if you want dedicated HSA-focused customer support and can tolerate a modest monthly fee.

Whichever account you choose, the worst move is keeping your HSA parked in the default cash position. Even modest monthly contributions invested in a low-cost S&P 500 index fund grow significantly over a 20-year horizon — and every dollar of qualified medical expenses you pay from the HSA is effectively a tax-free dollar spent.

faqs.question: Can I have an HSA if my employer already contributes to one?
faqs.answer: Yes. Employer contributions count toward your annual IRS contribution limit ($4,300 for self-only, $8,550 for family in 2026), but you are free to open a separate HSA at a provider of your choice and do a trustee-to-trustee transfer from your employer-sponsored account to consolidate funds.

faqs.question: What happens to my HSA if I switch to a non-HDHP health plan?
faqs.answer: You can no longer make new contributions once you are no longer enrolled in a qualifying high-deductible health plan, but the existing balance remains yours forever. You can still invest it, spend it on qualified medical expenses tax-free, or after age 65 withdraw it for any reason (taxed as ordinary income, like a traditional IRA).

faqs.question: Is it worth investing my HSA rather than spending it on current medical bills?
faqs.answer: If you can afford to pay current medical expenses out of pocket, keeping receipts and reimbursing yourself years later is a powerful strategy — sometimes called the HSA reimbursement hack. Your invested balance compounds tax-free, and there is no deadline to claim reimbursement, so a bill from 2026 can be reimbursed in 2036.

faqs.question: What counts as a qualified medical expense?
faqs.answer: The IRS list is broad: doctor visits, prescriptions, dental work, vision care, mental health therapy, and even certain over-the-counter items like menstrual products and sunscreen qualify. Non-qualified withdrawals before age 65 trigger income tax plus a 20% penalty, so keep records.

faqs.question: Can I use my HSA to pay Medicare premiums?
faqs.answer: Yes, once you are enrolled in Medicare (typically at 65), you can use your HSA to pay Medicare Part B, Part D, and Medicare Advantage premiums tax-free. You cannot use it to pay Medigap supplement premiums, however.

products.review: Fidelity charges absolutely nothing — no monthly fee, no investment threshold, no transfer fee — while offering access to thousands of mutual funds and ETFs including Fidelity's own zero-expense-ratio index funds. The FDIC-insured cash core earns a competitive yield tied to money market rates, and the mobile app lets you invest, pay bills, and view claims in one place. For most individual HSA shoppers, Fidelity is the obvious default.
pros: $0 monthly fee with no minimum balance requirement
Access to zero-expense-ratio index funds (e.g., FZROX at 0.00%)
Competitive cash yield on uninvested balances
cons: Not available as employer-sponsored plan for most small businesses
Investment research tools less specialized for HSA planning than dedicated HSA platforms

products.review: Optum Bank is one of the largest HSA custodians in the US and the default provider for millions of employer-sponsored plans, which means your HR contribution may land here automatically. The $2.75/month fee ($33/year) is waived when your balance stays above $3,000, and you get access to a curated mutual fund menu once you clear that threshold. The mobile app integrates with UnitedHealth claim data if you are on a UHC plan, which cuts down on manual receipt entry.
pros: Seamless integration with UnitedHealthcare insurance claims
Fee waived at $3,000 balance — realistic for most long-term savers
Strong employer-plan distribution makes rollovers unnecessary for many users
cons: Investment menu is narrower and higher-cost than Fidelity's lineup

products.review: Lively launched as a direct Fidelity rival — zero monthly fees, no minimum balance to invest, and a clean fintech-style interface that many users find cleaner than Fidelity's more complex dashboard. Investments are held through TD Ameritrade (now Schwab), giving access to a broad ETF marketplace. Lively also offers a dedicated HSA-linked debit card with digital wallet support and a receipt-capture feature that makes the IRS-documentation game easier.
pros: $0 monthly fee with no minimum to start investing
Receipt capture and expense tracking built into the app
HSA-linked debit card with Apple Pay and Google Pay support
cons: Smaller brand may concern users who prefer a legacy financial institution
Cash interest rate slightly lower than Fidelity's money market core

products.review: Further (formerly SelectAccount) has been a specialist HSA provider for over 20 years and shows it in the depth of its educational resources and customer support staff. Fees range from $1 to $4 per month depending on the plan tier, with higher tiers unlocking investment access and priority phone support with HSA-specialist advisors. The investment menu includes solid Vanguard and Dimensional funds, but the fee drag puts Further behind the free options for most self-directed savers.
pros: HSA-specialist phone and chat support with deep benefits expertise
Vanguard and Dimensional fund options at higher plan tiers
Strong employer and benefits administrator relationships for group plans
cons: $1–$4/month fee makes it more expensive than Fidelity or Lively over time
Fee structure requires careful tier selection to avoid overpaying for features you don't need

products.review: HealthEquity is the second-largest HSA custodian in the US by assets and serves major Fortune 500 companies, which is why many workers end up here through their employer. The $3.95/month fee ($47.40/year) is steep compared to free alternatives, but it is often subsidized by employers in group plans. Investment access starts after a $1,000 cash balance, which is lower than Optum's threshold, and the fund lineup includes low-cost Vanguard index funds once you clear that bar.
pros: Investment access begins at a $1,000 cash balance
Vanguard index funds available in the investment lineup
Robust employer dashboard for HR teams managing large groups
cons: $3.95/month fee is the highest among the five providers tested
Individual signup outside employer plans is less competitive vs. Fidelity/Lively

methodology: Accounts were evaluated on monthly fees and waiver thresholds, investment menu quality (fund count, expense ratios), cash APY, FDIC/SIPC coverage, minimum-to-invest requirements, mobile app functionality, and ease of trustee-to-trustee transfer.
pinDescription: Stop leaving HSA money on the table — these 5 best health savings accounts of 2026 slash fees and grow your tax-free balance faster.
